newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Possible Fokker saviour silent on Malaysian option.
newsitem.headline: Possible Fokker saviour silent on Malaysian option.

text.p: Begemann NV, named as the last potential saviour for bankrupt Fokker NV, declined to comment on Thursday on media reports that it was seeking Malaysian investment to relaunch the Dutch aircraft maker.

Court-appointed administrators who have been running Fokker since its bankruptcy in March said in a public report that they were still talking to Begemann chairman Andre Deleye about a last-ditch bid to revive Fokker.
But officials at Begemann declined to make any comment on its plans for Fokker, including the latest reports of possible Malaysian involvement in the project.
Stork NV, which acquired profitable Fokker units kept ouside the bankruptcy, has confirmed that it is taking part, at Deleye's invitation, in discussions to revive Fokker.
Company spokesman Koos Huurdeman declined to make any comment about the identity of others taking part in the talks.
But Dutch and Malaysian newspapers have reported that the Malaysian government and Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad himself are involved in the negotiations.
"We are looking at it. If it is feasible and viable, yes," Mahathir was quoted as saying by Business Times daily in response to questions from reporters on Wednesday.
Asked whether there was a deadline for the rescue plan, he said the government, through its investment arm Khazanah Holdings Bhd, was given a period of time to study the proposal.
"It is not a deadline but a limited time for us to study (the proposal)," Mahathir said.
At another function, Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim told reporters the government had not made any commitment on the rescue plan.
"We are just looking at the proposal and we are negotiating. There is no firm commitment," Anwar was quoted as saying by New Straits Times daily.

The Fokker administrators said in their report they had opened talks with Begemann chairman Deleye after rescue talks with South Korea's Samsung Aerospace broke down in November. The talks with Deleye are still in progress.
The administrators added that plans put forward by other interested parties had been rejected as unfeasible.
The Fokker factory near Amsterdam has continued to work on a handful of outstanding orders since the bankruptcy but the last four planes are due to be delivered between March and May.
The administrators said that while talks with Deleye were continuing they were also preparing to sell off Fokker's assets
